items.prompt: State what is meant by the term polysaccharide.
items.canonical_answer: A polysaccharide is a molecule made of many monosaccharides (sugar units) joined together by glycosidic bonds.
marking_guidance: 1 mark for the definition with both key words: many monosaccharides (or sugar units) and glycosidic bonds.
A statement that gives only 'a large carbohydrate' does not carry the key words and earns no mark.

items.prompt: State the position of the -OH group on carbon 1 in β-glucose, when the ring is drawn in the usual way with the CH2OH group on carbon 5 above the ring.
items.canonical_answer: The -OH on carbon 1 is above the ring, on the same side as the CH2OH group.
marking_guidance: 1 mark for above the ring (accept on the same side as the CH2OH group).
This is the one feature that separates β-glucose from α-glucose, where the -OH on carbon 1 is below the ring; a point that says 'below' earns no mark.
items.provenance: Authored from the topic 2.4.1 claim ledger and the syllabus learning outcomes. Scenarios, data and answers are our own. Unverified.

items.prompt: Describe how the structures of α-glucose and β-glucose are alike and how they differ.
items.canonical_answer: Both are isomers with the formula C6H12O6 and one ring of five carbon atoms and one oxygen atom, with a CH2OH group on carbon 5. They differ in the -OH on carbon 1, which is below the ring in α-glucose and above the ring in β-glucose, because the same atoms are arranged differently at that carbon.
marking_guidance: 2 marks: how they are alike, the same formula and one ring (1); how they differ, the position of the -OH on carbon 1, below the ring in α-glucose and above it in β-glucose (1).

A difference stated as the number of rings is the error the register records; both have one ring. The reason the forms are isomers, the same atoms arranged differently, is a further creditworthy point, but the tariff is 2.
items.provenance: Authored from the topic 2.4.1 claim ledger and the syllabus learning outcomes. Scenarios, data and answers are our own. Unverified.
objective_titles: describe and draw the ring forms of α-glucose and ᵦ-glucose

items.prompt: A learner says that α-glucose has one ring and β-glucose has two rings, because β-glucose has a -COOH group. Explain the error.
items.canonical_answer: The error is a confusion of the ring and the groups. In fact both forms have one ring, and glucose has hydroxyl groups (-OH), not a carboxyl group (-COOH). They differ only in the -OH on carbon 1. The test is to ask where the -OH on carbon 1 is: below the ring in α-glucose and above the ring in β-glucose.
marking_guidance: 2 marks: the error named, that the number of rings or a carboxyl group is said to separate the forms, when both have one ring and glucose has -OH, not -COOH (1); the correct idea or the test, that the forms differ in the position of the -OH on carbon 1, below the ring in α and above it in β (1).
The card is a discrimination between the error and the correct idea, not a repeat of the structure of glucose.

items.prompt:
The table gives the position of the -OH group on each ring carbon in two molecules, X and Y. Both molecules have the formula C6H12O6 and one ring. Describe what the table shows about the structures of X and Y, and identify which molecule is α-glucose.

| Carbon | -OH position in X | -OH position in Y |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | below the ring | above the ring |
| 2 | below the ring | below the ring |
| 3 | above the ring | above the ring |
| 4 | below the ring | below the ring |
items.canonical_answer: The table shows that X and Y have the -OH in the same positions on carbons 2, 3 and 4 and differ only at carbon 1. X has the -OH below the ring on carbon 1, so X is α-glucose, and Y, with the -OH above the ring, is β-glucose.
marking_guidance: 2 marks: the table shows that the positions are the same on carbons 2, 3 and 4 and differ only on carbon 1 (1); X is α-glucose because its -OH on carbon 1 is below the ring (1).
The reading must use the data in the table: it means that the two molecules are isomers that differ at carbon 1, and the answer gives the carbons by number.

items.prompt: Describe, in order, how a molecule of sucrose forms from its two monosaccharides.
items.canonical_answer: First, an -OH group on carbon 1 of α-glucose lines up with an -OH group on carbon 2 of fructose. Then the two -OH groups react in a condensation reaction, and a molecule of water is released. Finally, a glycosidic bond (a C-O-C link) joins carbon 1 of glucose to carbon 2 of fructose. The result is the disaccharide sucrose and one molecule of water.
marking_guidance: 3 marks, one for each step in the correct order: an -OH on each monosaccharide reacts (1); a molecule of water is released in this condensation reaction (1); a glycosidic bond forms between carbon 1 of glucose and carbon 2 of fructose, giving sucrose (1).
The sequence is the point: first the reaction, then the loss of water, finally the bond that is the result. A statement of the product without the condensation earns no mark for the step.

objective_titles: describe the formation of a glycosidic bond by condensation,with reference both to polysaccharides and to disaccharides, including sucrose

items.prompt: A cell makes an unbranched polysaccharide from 8 glucose units. Describe how the glucose units join, and state how many molecules of water are released.
items.canonical_answer: Condensation is repeated, adding one glucose unit at a time. Each time, an -OH group on the chain reacts with an -OH group on the next unit, a glycosidic bond forms and one molecule of water is released. For 8 units there are 8 - 1 = 7 glycosidic bonds, so 7 molecules of water are released.
marking_guidance: 2 marks: repeated condensation, one glycosidic bond and one water molecule for each unit added (1); 7 molecules of water, because 8 - 1 = 7 (1).
Accept 'one fewer bond than units' for the working. An answer of 8 water molecules counts a molecule per unit instead of per bond.

items.prompt:
The table gives our values for unbranched chains made by condensation of glucose units. Describe the pattern in the table and state how many glycosidic bonds are in an unbranched chain of 50 glucose units.

| Number of glucose units in the chain | Number of glycosidic bonds | Number of water molecules released |
|---|---|---|
| 2 | 1 | 1 |
| 4 | 3 | 3 |
| 6 | 5 | 5 |
| 8 | 7 | 7 |
items.canonical_answer: The table shows that the number of glycosidic bonds is one fewer than the number of glucose units, and that one molecule of water is released for each bond formed. For 50 units the chain has 50 - 1 = 49 glycosidic bonds.
marking_guidance: 2 marks: the pattern read from the data, bonds equal units minus one and one water per bond (1); 49 glycosidic bonds from 50 - 1 (1).
The answer reads the figures in the table, which show the pattern; a statement that gives 50 bonds counts one for each unit and earns no mark.

items.prompt: State what is meant by hydrolysis of a glycosidic bond.
items.canonical_answer: Hydrolysis of a glycosidic bond is the breaking of the bond by the addition of a molecule of water.
marking_guidance: 1 mark for the definition with the key words: breaking of the bond and addition of water.
A statement that hydrolysis 'releases water' is the wrong way round: water is used up, and is released in condensation.

items.prompt: State the feature of the structure of sucrose that makes it a non-reducing sugar.
items.canonical_answer: Both groups that could reduce copper(II) ions, on carbon 1 of glucose and carbon 2 of fructose, are used in the glycosidic bond.
marking_guidance: 1 mark for the feature: the reducing groups of both monosaccharides are used up in the glycosidic bond.
Accept 'it has no free reducing group'. A point that sucrose is a disaccharide or is not sweet earns no mark.

items.prompt:
The table gives our results of testing two sugar solutions, P and Q, with Benedict's solution, before and after boiling with dilute hydrochloric acid and neutralising. Describe what the results show about P and Q.

| Solution | Benedict's test before acid | Benedict's test after acid and neutralising |
|---|---|---|
| P | stays blue | brick-red precipitate |
| Q | stays blue | stays blue |
items.canonical_answer: The results show that P contains a non-reducing sugar and no detectable reducing sugar: it stays blue before the acid, and after hydrolysis the glycosidic bonds are broken and the reducing sugars released give a brick-red precipitate. Q contains neither a reducing sugar nor a non-reducing sugar, within the sensitivity of the test, because it stays blue both times.
marking_guidance: 2 marks: P contains a non-reducing sugar, because blue before and brick red after hydrolysis (1); Q contains neither, because blue in both tests (1).
The data are read together: the first result rules out a reducing sugar in the original sample, and the change after hydrolysis means that a glycosidic bond was broken.

items.prompt: State the type of bond that makes the branches in amylopectin.
items.canonical_answer: α-1,6 glycosidic bonds.
marking_guidance: 1 mark for α-1,6 glycosidic bonds (accept 1,6 glycosidic bonds).
A point that names α-1,4 bonds gives the bond in the chain, not the branch point.

items.prompt: Describe how the structure of glycogen suits it to its function as a store of glucose in muscle cells.
items.canonical_answer: Glycogen is highly branched, so it has many ends at which enzymes can hydrolyse glycosidic bonds at the same time, and glucose is released quickly when the muscle needs energy. The molecule is also compact, so a large amount of glucose is stored in a small space, and it is large and insoluble, so it does not diffuse out of the cell or change its water potential.
marking_guidance: 2 marks from three points: many branch ends, so enzymes act at many places at once and glucose is released quickly (1); compact, so a lot of glucose is stored in a small space (1); large and insoluble, so it does not leave the cell or change its water potential (1). The tariff is 2.
A point must say how the feature gives the function, because the structure is related to the function: 'it stores glucose' alone earns no mark.

items.prompt:
The table gives our approximate values for the branching of three polysaccharides of α-glucose. Describe what the table shows about branching, and state which polysaccharide would release glucose most quickly when an enzyme hydrolyses it.

| Polysaccharide | Branch points per 100 glucose units |
|---|---|
| amylose | 0 |
| amylopectin | 4 |
| glycogen | 9 |
items.canonical_answer: The table shows that branching increases from amylose, which has none, to amylopectin, with 4 branch points per 100 glucose units, to glycogen, with 9. Glycogen has the most branch ends, so an enzyme can hydrolyse it at the most places at once, and it would tend to release glucose most quickly.
marking_guidance: 2 marks: the increase in branching from 0 to 4 to 9 branch points per 100 units, read from the table (1); glycogen, because the most branch ends allow enzymes to act at the most places (1).
The reading uses the figures in the table, which means the order amylose, amylopectin, glycogen; a tendency, not a measured rate, is claimed.

items.prompt: State the type of bond that joins neighbouring cellulose chains to one another.
items.canonical_answer: Hydrogen bonds.
marking_guidance: 1 mark for hydrogen bonds.
Glycosidic bonds join the units inside a chain; that point earns no mark here.

items.prompt: Describe how the arrangement of cellulose molecules makes a plant cell wall strong.
items.canonical_answer: Cellulose chains are straight and unbranched and lie parallel to one another. A very large number of hydrogen bonds form between neighbouring chains, which holds them in microfibrils and fibres with high tensile strength. The fibres are laid in layers at different angles, so the wall resists stretching in more than one direction.
marking_guidance: 2 marks from three points: straight parallel chains (1); many hydrogen bonds between neighbouring chains forming microfibrils and fibres with high tensile strength (1); fibres in layers at different angles, so that stretching is resisted in more than one direction (1). The tariff is 2.
The points are about the arrangement and so name the hydrogen bonds between chains, not the bond in a chain.

items.prompt: A learner says that hydrogen bonds join the glucose units into a cellulose chain. Explain the error.
items.canonical_answer: The error is a confusion of the bonds within a chain with the bonds between chains. In fact the glucose units in a chain are joined by β-1,4 glycosidic bonds, and the hydrogen bonds act between neighbouring chains. The test is to ask which bond is within a chain and which is between chains.
marking_guidance: 2 marks: the error named, hydrogen bonds placed inside the chain instead of between chains (1); the correct idea, glycosidic bonds join the units in the chain and hydrogen bonds link neighbouring chains, or the test that separates them (1).
The card is a discrimination between two bonds, not a repeat of the structure of cellulose.

items.prompt: A learner says that cellulose is strong because it is insoluble and is not affected by pH. Explain what is wrong with this and state what gives a cellulose fibre its strength.
items.canonical_answer: The error is the wrong angle on the same idea. Solubility and pH are not what resists stretching. In fact the strength comes from the very large number of hydrogen bonds that hold parallel chains together in microfibrils. The test is to ask what holds the chains together to resist being pulled apart.
marking_guidance: 2 marks: the error named, that solubility or pH is given as the reason instead of the structure (1); the correct idea, many hydrogen bonds between parallel chains in microfibrils (1).
The test question is what holds the chains together; an answer that restates 'cellulose is strong' earns no mark.

items.prompt:
The table gives our values for two threads of equal thickness, one made from a plant fibre rich in cellulose and one made from dried starch. Describe what the data show and state the feature of cellulose structure that accounts for the difference.

| Thread | Mass hung from the thread when it broke (kg) |
|---|---|
| plant fibre rich in cellulose | 6.5 |
| dried starch | 0.4 |
items.canonical_answer: The data show that the cellulose-rich thread held 6.5 kg before it broke, which is 6.5 - 0.4 = 6.1 kg more than the 0.4 kg held by the starch thread. A feature of cellulose that accounts for this is the very large number of hydrogen bonds between its straight parallel chains, which gives the fibres high tensile strength.
marking_guidance: 2 marks: the comparison using the figures, 6.5 kg against 0.4 kg (1); the feature, many hydrogen bonds between straight parallel chains (1).
The data are two threads and a tendency is supported, not a rule; the feature named must be one of the structure, not solubility. The comparison means the difference is read from the data.

items.canonical_answer: An ester bond.

items.prompt: Describe how the three ester bonds in a triglyceride form.
items.canonical_answer: Each ester bond forms by condensation. The -COOH group of a fatty acid reacts with an -OH group on glycerol, a molecule of water is released and an ester bond forms. This happens three times, so three molecules of water are released for each triglyceride.
marking_guidance: 2 marks: condensation between the -COOH of a fatty acid and an -OH of glycerol, with water released (1); repeated for three fatty acids, giving three ester bonds and three molecules of water (1).
How the bond forms is the point, so the answer names the groups that react.

items.prompt: A learner says that the ester bonds in a triglyceride are the same as the glycosidic bonds in starch. Explain the error.
items.canonical_answer: The error is a confusion of two bonds. In fact ester bonds join fatty acids to glycerol in triglycerides, and glycosidic bonds join sugar units in carbohydrates. The test is to ask which bond joins sugars and which joins fatty acids to glycerol.
marking_guidance: 2 marks: the error named, ester and glycosidic bonds treated as the same (1); the correct idea, ester bonds join fatty acids to glycerol and glycosidic bonds join sugars, or the test that separates them (1).
The card is a discrimination between two bonds, not a repeat of the structure of a triglyceride.

items.prompt:
The table gives our approximate values for the energy released when a carbohydrate and a triglyceride are respired. Describe what the table shows and state how the structure of a triglyceride accounts for the difference.

| Substance | Energy released (kJ per g) |
|---|---|
| carbohydrate | 17 |
| triglyceride | 38 |
items.canonical_answer: The table shows that a gram of triglyceride releases 38 kJ, which is 38 - 17 = 21 kJ more than a gram of carbohydrate. The long hydrocarbon tails of the fatty acids contain a lot of C-H bonds, so more energy is released per gram, which makes a triglyceride a compact energy store.
marking_guidance: 2 marks: the comparison with figures, 38 kJ per g against 17 kJ per g (1); the structure, long hydrocarbon tails with many C-H bonds (1).
The data are read first and then the structure is related to the function; the values are ours and approximate. This means that a triglyceride releases more energy per gram.

items.canonical_answer: The phosphate group, which is the head of the molecule.
marking_guidance: 1 mark for the phosphate group (the head).

items.prompt: Explain why phospholipids form a bilayer in the cell surface membrane.
items.canonical_answer: Each phospholipid has a hydrophilic head and two hydrophobic tails. The heads face outwards into the water of the cytoplasm and of the surroundings, because they are attracted to water, and the tails face inwards, away from the water, because they are repelled by it. This gives a bilayer, one membrane with two layers of phospholipid.
marking_guidance: 2 marks: the heads are hydrophilic and so face the water on both sides (1); the tails are hydrophobic and so face inwards, away from the water (1).
The reason must be given with each part, the attraction to water or the repulsion from it, because the explanation links structure and function.

items.prompt:
The table gives our values for how quickly three substances cross a model phospholipid bilayer. Describe what the table shows and state the feature of the bilayer that accounts for it.

| Substance | Type of particle | Relative rate of crossing (arbitrary units) |
|---|---|---|
| oxygen | small, non-polar molecule | 100 |
| glucose | polar molecule | 2 |
| sodium ion | charged particle | 0.1 |
items.canonical_answer: The table shows that oxygen crosses fastest, at 100 units, glucose crosses much more slowly, at 2 units, and the sodium ion crosses slowest, at 0.1 units. This is because the centre of the bilayer is hydrophobic, so polar molecules and charged particles do not dissolve in it, while a small non-polar molecule does.
marking_guidance: 2 marks: the order of the rates read from the table, oxygen fastest, then glucose, then the sodium ion (1); the hydrophobic centre of the bilayer, in which polar and charged particles do not dissolve but non-polar molecules do (1).
The figures in the table are used; the values are ours and show a tendency for particles of these kinds. This means that the rate falls as the particle becomes more polar or charged.

items.prompt: Describe, in order, how to test a solution for a reducing sugar and what a positive result looks like.
items.canonical_answer: First, add Benedict's solution, which is blue, to a sample of the solution in a test tube. Then heat the tube in a water bath near boiling for several minutes. A positive result is a colour change from blue through green, yellow and orange to a brick-red precipitate, and the solution stays blue if no reducing sugar is present.
marking_guidance: 3 marks, in the correct order: Benedict's solution added to the sample (1); heated in a water bath near boiling for several minutes (1); the positive result, an orange or brick-red precipitate (1).
The sequence matters: heating comes after the reagent is added. The result stated without the heating step loses the heating mark.

items.prompt: State why a tube of distilled water is tested in the same way as the food samples in a Benedict's test.
items.canonical_answer: It is a control, so that it shows what a negative result looks like, with the reagent staying blue, so that a colour change in a sample can be put down to the sample.
marking_guidance: 1 mark for the reason: a control, showing the negative result (the reagent staying blue) for comparison.

items.prompt: Amylase is mixed with starch solution. After 20 minutes iodine solution is added to a sample of the mixture and stays yellow-brown. A learner concludes that sugar has formed. Explain the error.
items.canonical_answer: The error is a confusion of the evidence. In fact the yellow-brown colour shows only that starch is absent, and it says nothing about sugar. A reducing sugar is shown by a positive Benedict's test. The test is to ask whether the result is evidence that starch has gone or that sugar has appeared.
marking_guidance: 2 marks: the error named, a yellow-brown result with iodine read as evidence that sugar has formed (1); the correct idea, that it shows starch is absent and the sugar is shown by Benedict's test, or the test that separates them (1).
The card is a discrimination between two pieces of evidence, not a repeat of the iodine test.

items.prompt:
The table gives our results of three tests on three solutions, X, Y and Z. Describe what the results show about the food molecules in X, Y and Z.

| Solution | Benedict's test | Iodine test | Emulsion test |
|---|---|---|---|
| X | brick-red precipitate | yellow-brown | stays clear |
| Y | stays blue | blue-black | stays clear |
| Z | stays blue | yellow-brown | cloudy white |

Each point is read from the table and means that a test is positive: the colour is named with the molecule it shows.

items.prompt: Describe, in order, how to estimate the concentration of a reducing sugar solution by timing the first colour change with Benedict's solution.
items.canonical_answer: First, make a set of standard solutions of the same reducing sugar at known concentrations. Then add the same volume of Benedict's solution to the same volume of each standard and of the unknown, heat the tubes in a water bath at the same temperature, and record the time to the first colour change in each. Finally, plot a graph of time against concentration for the standards and read off the concentration that matches the time for the unknown.
marking_guidance: 3 marks, one for each step in the correct order: standards of known concentration made (1); same volumes and temperature, and the time to the first colour change recorded for each (1); graph or comparison with the standards used to estimate the unknown (1).
The estimate is the result of the comparison, so the unknown is tested last, in the same way as the standards.

items.prompt: State why the volume of Benedict's solution is kept the same in each tube in a semi-quantitative test.
items.canonical_answer: So that the concentration of reducing sugar is the only thing that differs between the tubes, because a different volume of reagent would change the time or colour, and the comparison would be unfair.
marking_guidance: 1 mark for the reason: only the concentration of sugar should differ, so any change in time or colour is caused by it.
The purpose is a fair comparison; 'to be accurate' on its own earns no mark.

items.prompt:
The table gives our results of timing the first colour change when standard glucose solutions are heated with Benedict's solution. An unknown solution gave a time of 135 s under the same conditions. Describe the pattern in the table and state the range in which the concentration of the unknown lies.

| Concentration of glucose (per cent) | Time to first colour change (s) |
|---|---|
| 0.125 | 410 |
| 0.25 | 270 |
| 0.5 | 170 |
| 1.0 | 100 |
| 2.0 | 55 |
items.canonical_answer: The table shows that the time to the first colour change decreases as the concentration of glucose increases. A time of 135 s lies between 170 s, for 0.5 per cent, and 100 s, for 1.0 per cent, so the unknown has a concentration between 0.5 and 1.0 per cent.
marking_guidance: 2 marks: the pattern read from the table, time decreasing as concentration increases (1); between 0.5 and 1.0 per cent, because 135 s lies between 170 s and 100 s (1).
The estimate is a range between two standards and is not an exact value. An answer that gives one figure such as 0.75 per cent is not supported by the data.

items.prompt: Describe, in order, how to test a solution for a non-reducing sugar.
items.canonical_answer: First, test a sample with Benedict's solution, which stays blue if no reducing sugar is present. Then boil a fresh sample with dilute hydrochloric acid, cool it and neutralise it with sodium hydrogencarbonate. Finally, add Benedict's solution and heat in a water bath: an orange or brick-red precipitate shows that a non-reducing sugar was present.
marking_guidance: 3 marks, in the correct order: a first Benedict's test is negative, so the sample stays blue (1); a fresh sample is boiled with dilute hydrochloric acid, then neutralised (1); Benedict's solution is added and heated, and a brick-red precipitate is the positive result (1).
The sequence is the point: the first test comes before the acid, and neutralising comes before the second Benedict's test.

items.prompt: State why the sample is neutralised after boiling with dilute hydrochloric acid and before Benedict's solution is added.
items.canonical_answer: Benedict's solution works in alkaline conditions, so acid left in the sample would stop the reaction and give a false negative.
marking_guidance: 1 mark for the reason: Benedict's solution needs alkaline conditions, so acid would prevent the colour change.
The purpose is the reaction conditions; 'to make it safe' is not the reason and earns no mark.

items.prompt: A student has a 2.0 per cent solution of glucose and an unknown solution of glucose. Describe, in order, how the student makes standards of 1.0, 0.5 and 0.25 per cent and uses them to estimate the concentration of the unknown.
items.canonical_answer: First, mix 10 cm3 of the 2.0 per cent solution with 10 cm3 of distilled water to make 1.0 per cent. Then mix 10 cm3 of that with 10 cm3 of water to make 0.5 per cent, and repeat to make 0.25 per cent. Finally, test each standard and the unknown in the same way with Benedict's solution, with the same volumes, temperature and heating time, and compare the colour or the time to the first colour change of the unknown with the standards.
marking_guidance: 3 marks, in the correct order: equal volumes of solution and water, which halve the concentration (1); the step repeated to make 0.5 and 0.25 per cent (1); each standard and the unknown tested in the same way and compared (1).
The result is the estimate between standards, and the dilution steps come first. Volumes in the right proportion (equal volumes) are the working.

items.prompt: State why an unknown solution is diluted by a known factor when its result is stronger than that of the strongest standard.
items.canonical_answer: Its result is outside the range of the standards and cannot be compared with them; the diluted solution can be compared, and its estimate multiplied by the dilution factor gives the concentration of the original.
marking_guidance: 1 mark for the reason: the result is outside the range of the standards, so it cannot be compared until it is diluted.
The purpose is to bring the unknown into the range of the standards; the dilution factor is then used to multiply the estimate.

items.prompt:
Twelve questions. Choose one option for each.

1. Which type of reaction forms a glycosidic bond between two monosaccharides?
A  hydrolysis
B  condensation
C  oxidation
D  neutralisation

2. Two α-glucose units join to form maltose. How many molecules of water are released?
A  0
B  2
C  3
D  1

3. An unbranched chain is made from 6 monosaccharides by condensation. How many glycosidic bonds does it contain?
A  5
B  6
C  7
D  12

4. Which bond makes the side branches in amylopectin?
A  α-1,4 glycosidic bonds
B  β-1,4 glycosidic bonds
C  α-1,6 glycosidic bonds
D  hydrogen bonds

5. Why is glycogen well suited to storing glucose in muscle cells?
A  It is soluble, so it diffuses quickly
B  It is made of β-glucose, so enzymes cannot act on it
C  It is unbranched and so is tightly packed
D  It has many branch ends, so enzymes can release glucose quickly.

6. Which statement about starch is correct?
A  Amylose is branched and amylopectin is not
B  Amylose and amylopectin are both polymers of α-glucose.
C  Starch is made of β-glucose
D  Starch is the main energy store of animals

7. What joins the glucose units within one cellulose chain?
A  hydrogen bonds
B  ester bonds
C  β-1,4 glycosidic bonds
D  α-1,4 glycosidic bonds

8. Which feature gives a cellulose fibre its high tensile strength?
A  many hydrogen bonds between neighbouring parallel chains
B  glycosidic bonds between chains
C  solubility in water
D  regular branches along the chain

9. Each β-glucose unit in a cellulose chain is turned through 180° relative to its neighbour. What is the result?
A  a coiled helix
B  a straight, unbranched chain
C  a chain with branches
D  a closed ring of glucose units

10. A clear sugar solution stays blue when heated with Benedict's solution. After boiling a fresh sample with dilute hydrochloric acid and neutralising it, Benedict's solution gives a brick-red precipitate. What does the solution contain?
A  a reducing sugar that was present from the start
B  no sugar of any kind
C  a lipid
D  a non-reducing sugar

11. Iodine solution is added to a mixture in which an enzyme has acted on starch. It stays yellow-brown. What does this show?
A  starch is absent
B  sugar has formed
C  a reducing sugar is present
D  lipid is present

12. A sample is shaken with ethanol and then poured into water. The mixture stays clear. What does this show?
A  lipid is present
B  starch is present
C  no lipid is present
D  a reducing sugar is present
items.canonical_answer:
Key: 1 B, 2 D, 3 A, 4 C, 5 D, 6 B, 7 C, 8 A, 9 B, 10 D, 11 A, 12 C.
1. condensation (B). A is the reverse reaction, which breaks the bond using water; C is no oxygen is added in joining sugar units; D is an acid-base reaction, unrelated to joining sugars.
2. 1 (D). A is the error of thinking water is added, as in hydrolysis; B is one water for each glucose unit, instead of one for each bond; C is no basis in the reaction.
3. 5 (A). B is one bond counted for each unit instead of 6 - 1; C is one more than the number of units; D is two bonds counted for each unit.
4. α-1,6 glycosidic bonds (C). A is the bond in the chains, not at the branch points; B is the bond in cellulose; D is these act between cellulose chains, not at branches in starch.
5. It has many branch ends, so enzymes can release glucose quickly. (D). A is it is insoluble, which is a reason it suits storage; B is it is made of α-glucose; C is glycogen is highly branched.
6. Amylose and amylopectin are both polymers of α-glucose. (B). A is amylose is the unbranched molecule; C is that is cellulose; D is animals store glycogen.
7. β-1,4 glycosidic bonds (C). A is these act between chains, the error in the register; B is these join fatty acids to glycerol, not sugar units; D is the bond in amylose, not in cellulose.
8. many hydrogen bonds between neighbouring parallel chains (A). B is these act inside a chain, not between chains; C is not a cause of resistance to stretching; D is cellulose is unbranched.
9. a straight, unbranched chain (B). A is the shape of amylose; C is branches form in amylopectin and glycogen; D is a cellulose chain does not close into a ring.
10. a non-reducing sugar (D). A is it would have given a precipitate in the first test; B is the second test is positive; C is the emulsion test, not Benedict's test, detects lipids.
11. starch is absent (A). B is iodine does not detect sugar, the error in the register; C is that needs a Benedict's test; D is that needs an emulsion test.
12. no lipid is present (C). A is lipid would give a cloudy white emulsion; B is starch is detected with iodine solution; D is that needs Benedict's test.
marking_guidance: The key: one mark per correct option, twelve marks in all; about half the questions test recall and half test application to a described result, count or structure.

Each distractor is a named error: hydrolysis for condensation, a bond counted per unit, the bond in the chain for the branch bond, hydrogen bonds placed inside the chain (the misconception register first), a brown iodine result read as sugar.

items.prompt:
A class in Rundu tests three sugar solutions, P, Q and R. These are our results.

| Solution | Benedict's test | Iodine test | Benedict's test after boiling with dilute hydrochloric acid and neutralising |
|---|---|---|---|
| P | stays blue | yellow-brown | brick-red precipitate |
| Q | brick-red precipitate | yellow-brown | brick-red precipitate |
| R | stays blue | blue-black | not done |

(a) State which solution contains starch. [1]
(b) Describe what the results for P show about the sugar in P. [2]
(c) Explain why the sample of P is neutralised before the second Benedict's test. [2]
(d) Describe what happens to the glycosidic bond in sucrose when it is hydrolysed, state the two monosaccharides released, and name the type of reaction by which the bond was formed. [3]
items.canonical_answer:
(a) R.
(b) P contains a non-reducing sugar. It stays blue in the first test, so it has no detectable reducing sugar, and after boiling with acid it gives a brick-red precipitate, because hydrolysis has broken the glycosidic bond and released reducing sugars.
(c) Benedict's solution works in alkaline conditions, so acid left in the sample would stop the reaction, because the colour change would not occur, and the result would be a false negative.
(d) The glycosidic bond is broken by the addition of a molecule of water. The monosaccharides released are glucose and fructose. The bond was formed by a condensation reaction, in which water was released.
marking_guidance: Marks and points: (a) 1 mark for R; (b) 2 marks from three points: stays blue at first, so no reducing sugar; brick red after acid, so reducing sugars were released; so P contains a non-reducing sugar; (c) 2 marks from three points: Benedict's solution needs alkaline conditions; acid would stop the reaction; a false negative would result; (d) 3 marks: bond broken by the addition of water (hydrolysis); glucose and fructose; formed by condensation.
Parts (a) and (d) credit AO A (4 marks); parts (b) and (c) credit AO B (4 marks). The reasoning in (b) uses the data for P in the table, and the answer to (d) is stated as a term for each point.
